How cutting creates pace. I edit to a beat for music videos, which helps and hurts on narrative work. The soundtrack side is in [[Sound design]].

## Murch's Rule of Six

From "In the Blink of an Eye" (1995). What a cut should serve, in order of weight: emotion 51%, story 23%, rhythm 10%, eye-trace 7%, two-dimensional plane of the screen 5%, three-dimensional space 4%. If you have to break one, break from the bottom. I break rhythm far too often because the musician in me wants every cut on a downbeat.

## Cutting on the blink

Murch again: people blink when a thought finishes, so a good actor's blink is a natural cut point. Watched Gene Hackman in "The Conversation" (1974) with the sound off and it holds up.

## Shot length

- "Man with a Movie Camera" (1929): average shot about 2.3 s, and that's 1929. See [[Documentary picks]].
- "The Bourne Ultimatum" (2007): around 1.9 s. Exhausting.
- "Tokyo Story" (1953): long, long takes. Ozu lets the shot finish its thought.
- Our "Saltcoats" video (Kirsty Duncan, 104 BPM): cuts every two bars, 4.6 s, then every bar in the last chorus, 2.3 s. The doubling felt like the song lifting.

## Sound leading the picture

J-cut: next scene's sound starts before its picture. L-cut: this scene's sound carries over the next picture. Almost every dialogue scene in a feature does one or the other. In our short, the tram bell from the final scene comes in under Margaret's kitchen, three seconds early.

## Kuleshov

Same neutral face, cut against soup, a coffin, a child. The audience reads hunger, grief, love. Showed the club a recreation before "Rashomon" (see [[Kurosawa]]) and Jim Halloran said "so the actor doesn't matter". Not what I said.

## Tools

DaVinci Resolve 19, free version, on the studio PC. Proxies at 1080p, timeline at 25 fps. Shortcut I wish I'd learned sooner: Ctrl+B to blade at the playhead.
